passages.title: First Rounds
passages.text:
Thursday, the last one in October, and my first evening rounds alone at the Marlowe Creek Wildlife Sanctuary.

Head Keeper Whitlock handed me the clipboard at six o'clock and repeated the rule she gives to every new keeper.  Count everything twice, she said, and record what you actually observe, never what you expect to observe.  I told her that I understood her perfectly.  That was not entirely true then, although it is finally true tonight.

Evening rounds begin at the top of the hill and work downward toward the creek.  The barn owls come first, because they are awake and impatient before anything else in the sanctuary stirs.  After the owls come the two red foxes, who pretend to be sleeping until the moment their food bowl lands.  After the foxes comes the otter pool, where Rana ordinarily meets me at the glass with her whiskers flattened against it.  She did not meet me this evening.  I almost failed to write that down, because at the time it seemed like nothing worth recording.

The path bends past the marsh boardwalk afterward, and although you cannot see much of the marsh after dark, you can hear absolutely all of it.  The insects begin in one corner and spread until the entire basin is ringing with them.  Something large moved through the reeds while I was standing there, slowly and completely unbothered, and I never did see what it was.  Instead of guessing, I recorded the time, 7:41, and continued walking down the hill.

The tortoise yard is the final stop before the gate, and three desert tortoises live there on a slope of packed sand and low brush.  Their names are Juniper, Ada, and Salt.  Whitlock believes the tortoise yard teaches a new keeper more than any other stop on the route, because nothing inside it ever happens quickly.  You have to slow yourself down deliberately in order to count animals that refuse to move.

I counted two.

I counted a second time, exactly the way she had instructed me, and arrived at two again.  A tortoise is not a bird and cannot simply leave.  A wall of buried block surrounds that yard, sunk deeper than any of them could possibly dig.  Even so, the yard in front of me held two tortoises while the sheet in my hand insisted on three.

The gate log at the bottom of the hill wanted a signature and a time, and I stood there holding the pen without signing anything.  Every part of me wanted to write down three, because three was the comfortable number that would have let me go home.  Whitlock's rule kept getting in the way of my pen.

I wrote down two instead, and then I picked up the radio.

That is the entire first lesson of this job, as far as I can determine.  The sheet is not a wish.  The sheet is a record, and a record can only help somebody later if it was honest at the moment somebody wrote it.

passages.title: The Count That Would Not Close
passages.text:
Bo Ferris answered the radio on my second call.  He never once suggested that I had simply miscounted, which I appreciated more than he knows.  He promised to meet me at the tortoise yard with the yard binder, and he told me not to climb the wall or start digging anywhere.  Then he added one more instruction that I have been thinking about ever since.  Do not fix the number, he said, and do not improve it either.  Bring me the number you actually got.

We searched the enclosure in a slow grid, shoulder to shoulder, with our hands out of our pockets.  Ada was underneath the feeding shelf, half buried in sand that still held the afternoon's warmth.  Salt was pressed against the north wall with her head tucked completely inside her shell.  Juniper was nowhere at all.  I looked in every place a tortoise could reasonably fit, and several places where a tortoise could not.  Ferris ran his flashlight along the base of the slope and said nothing whatsoever for a long while.

Whitlock arrived at ten minutes past eight with the yard binder under her arm.  She did not ask me whether I was certain.  She asked what time I had counted, whether the yard lights had been burning, and how the surface of the sand had felt.  Cooler than last week, I told her, and she nodded as though that answered something.

She opened the binder to the tortoise section and turned it around so that I could read it myself.  Halfway down the page, in handwriting that was four years old, somebody had recorded a note about Juniper.  Juniper digs, the note said, and Juniper has always dug.  During her first autumn at the sanctuary she went under the east slope and remained underground for nineteen days, and every keeper on the evening shift aged a decade.

Underneath that entry, in a different color of ink, somebody had drawn a careful little map.  It marked the mouth of a burrow behind the manzanita at the eastern corner.  It estimated the depth in feet, and it said, in capital letters, DO NOT DIG HER OUT.

The three of us walked to the eastern corner together.  The manzanita had grown out across the sand in the years since the map was drawn.  The burrow mouth sat in its shadow, dark and round and exactly where the page had promised it would be.  Ferris crouched down and held the back of his hand near the opening for a moment.  Warmer than the air out here, he reported.  She is home.

I asked how long she intended to stay under.  Whitlock said the honest answer is that nobody can tell you, because that decision is her business rather than ours.  Then she took my clipboard, wrote down the number two, and beside it recorded a full line about the burrow, the time, and the keeper who had checked it.

The count still would not close, and Whitlock told me that was perfectly fine.  A count that refuses to close is not a failure, she explained.  It is a question you have written down carefully enough that the next keeper can actually answer it.

passages.title: Under the Hill
passages.text:
She began the hole on the day the light changed.

Nothing told her to dig, exactly.  The wanting simply arrived the way hunger arrives, and her front legs answered it without asking permission.  They are not delicate legs.  They are flat and scaled and built for moving ground, and they moved ground steadily all morning.  Sand traveled backward past her shell in small tired heaps, and roots surrendered with a sound like thread breaking.  The hole became a tunnel that bent once and took away the last of the sky.

Inside the tunnel the air stopped moving altogether, which is the first gift a burrow gives anybody.  Above her the day would swing from hot to cold and back again, and none of that swinging reached her.  Down here the air remained cool and slightly damp whether the sun was up or gone.  Her breathing slowed, and then everything else slowed along with it.

She could still feel the world arriving through the floor.  Feet crossed the yard above her twice every day, heavy ones and lighter ones.  A cart rolled along the path each evening, and its sound reached her legs before it reached anything else.  Once, something dragged for a long time near the mouth of the tunnel, and she drew her head back and waited until the dragging went away.

She was not hiding, exactly, because hiding is a thing an animal does about something.  This was a season instead, and she was going down into it the way water goes downhill.

Her body had already begun putting itself away for the cold months ahead.  She had eaten generously through the green weeks, the grasses and the weeds and the flat pads she had to work at patiently.  Now food had stopped interesting her entirely.  Her heart slowed, and her breathing slowed until a person watching from the surface would have waited a long while to see her sides move at all.  Nothing hurt anywhere, and nothing whatsoever was wrong.  She was becoming extremely still, on purpose, for a very long time.

Light reached the bend of the tunnel occasionally, thin and gray, and never once reached her.  Sometimes a beam swung across the opening and traveled away again.  Sometimes the ground carried voices, low and rising and falling together, and lately one of those voices was new.

The new voice came back many evenings in a row.  It stopped at the manzanita each time and stood there without ever digging.  She did not understand what standing there was supposed to mean.  She knew only the shape of it in the ground, arriving and leaving and arriving again, while the cold went on settling into the hill above her and she went on going still.

passages.title: The Otter Diet Card, Annotated
passages.text:
Every animal at Marlowe Creek has a diet card, and a diet card is not a suggestion.  It is the record of what that animal eats, who fed it, and when.  I copied Rana's card into this notebook on Tuesday, the first of February, and wrote my own notes under each block.  Rana is our North American river otter, eleven years old, and she has been slow for days now.

The heading reads: RANA, river otter, enclosure four, two feeds daily, 7:00 and 15:30.

The first block lists the food.  It calls for four hundred grams of capelin, three hundred grams of herring, and two hundred grams of whole rainbow trout.  Under the fish comes a line the card sets apart inside its own box.  Thiamine supplement, one tablet, crushed into the first feed, daily, no exceptions.

The second block is the part keepers fill in themselves.  It is a grid of small squares, one square for every feed, and a keeper initials the square once the feeding is done.  The card also asks for a separate initial in a narrow column beside the grid.  That narrow column is only for the supplement.  Two initials, one feeding, and the design is deliberate.  Whitlock says a single initial lets a person remember the fish and forget the tablet.

Here is what I found reading down every line of that narrow column for the past two weeks, top to bottom, without skipping any.  Fourteen days of feeding produced twenty-eight fish squares, and every one of them was initialed.  The supplement column beside them carries initials on three days.

The third block is the one I did not understand at first.  It reads: fish drawn from front freezer only, oldest lot first, blue tag before white tag.  Beneath that instruction, in smaller type, the card explains what the two tags mean.  A blue tag marks a lot packed during the current season.  A white tag marks a lot held much longer, and any white-tag lot must be pulled and checked by a keeper before anybody thaws it.

I asked Hollis Vance in the feed room about the front freezer.  He told me the front unit has been down since the eleventh of January, waiting on a part.  The whole thaw list, he explained, has been coming out of freezer two in the back of the building instead.  When I asked what the tags in freezer two look like, he thought for a second and then admitted, honestly, mostly white.

That is the point where I stopped taking notes and went looking for the veterinarian.

passages.title: Lethargy Workup: Rana
passages.text:
Our veterinarian leaves her memos in the keeper room inside a plain folder, and she expects everyone to read them.  Here is Tuesday's memo, copied out with her permission, with the passages I had to look up rewritten in my own words.

Patient: Rana, river otter, eleven years.  Reason for workup: lethargy, four days.

Her findings come first.  Rana is still eating, but slowly.  She has begun leaving fish in the pool for the first time in years.  She entered the water late at both feeds and hauled herself out early.  Her weight has dropped slightly since the last weigh-in.  Her eyes, ears, teeth, and coat all look normal, and she has no fever, no wound, and no swelling anywhere.  Blood was drawn Tuesday afternoon and sent to the outside laboratory.

Then comes the section of the memo that matters most.  In any animal fed a diet of raw frozen fish, the memo says, low energy and a fading appetite should always raise the question of thiamine.  Thiamine is a vitamin, sometimes called B1, and an animal needs it in order to turn food into usable energy.  A body cannot store very much of it, so a shortage announces itself in weeks rather than years.

The reason fish-eating animals are the ones at risk is an enzyme called thiaminase.  Many kinds of fish carry thiaminase naturally, and the enzyme does exactly one thing: it breaks thiamine apart.  Freezing slows that enzyme down considerably, but freezing does not destroy it.  The longer a fish sits frozen, the more thiamine the enzyme removes.  A fish frozen last month is not the same food as a fish frozen a year ago, even though the two look identical on the tray.  Heat does destroy thiaminase, which is why cooking would end the problem, and nobody cooks a river otter's dinner.

That is the reason the diet card carries a thiamine tablet inside its own box.  It is also the reason the feed room is supposed to rotate its stock, rather than reaching for whatever container sits closest.  The supplement exists to replace what the enzyme removes.

The memo then lists the signs she is watching for, in the order they generally appear.  Slowness and appetite loss arrive first.  In an animal left short for longer, trouble with balance and coordination follows, and that is the stage where the problem stops being easy to reverse.  Her note adds, in her own handwriting, that she would far rather look foolish this week than clever next month.

Her final line is a request rather than a diagnosis.  She asks for two records: the supplement column from Rana's diet card, and the freezer paperwork showing which lot the last three weeks of fish came out of.

I already had the first record in my notebook, so I went looking for the second one.

passages.title: The Cold-Chain Invoice
passages.text:
The freezer paperwork lives in a feed-room binder that everybody here calls the cold chain.  The name means exactly what it sounds like.  Fish is supposed to remain frozen in an unbroken line from the boat to the tray.  Every pair of hands it passes through signs for it along the way.  I copied out the two invoices covering the deliveries this feed room has taken in since the start of January.

The first invoice, dated the eighth of January, records twelve cases of capelin from Harrow Bay Seafood.  The lot number is 4471, packed on the fourth of December, received by Hollis Vance and stored in the front freezer under a blue tag.

The second invoice is the one that stopped me.  It is dated the eleventh of January, the same day the front freezer failed.  It also carries a word stamped in the corner that the first invoice does not have anywhere: CLEARANCE.  This one records eighteen cases of capelin under lot number 3902, packed in November of the year before last.  Hollis Vance received it and stored it in freezer two, beneath a white tag with the notation check before use.

Fourteen months sat between that lot's packing date and the afternoon it arrived in our feed room.

Our own rule at Marlowe Creek is six months in the freezer, oldest lot first.  Every white-tag lot is pulled and inspected by a keeper before anybody thaws it.  That particular rule belongs to us, written on the inside cover of the cold chain binder.  It is a sanctuary policy rather than a law of nature.  What does not belong to us is the biological reason behind the rule.  The veterinarian explained that reason in her memo, and it does not care whose binder it happens to be written in.

The final section of the binder is the thaw log, and the thaw log is where the two halves of this case finally meet.  Every entry from the twelfth of January onward names the same source freezer, freezer two.  Every entry names the identical lot, 3902.  There are nineteen such entries altogether, one for each thaw, each initialed and timed, and the last of them is dated the thirtieth.

So the picture assembled from paperwork alone, before any blood test comes back, looks something like this.  For nineteen days in a row, Rana ate fish that had been sitting frozen for more than a year.  On sixteen of those same days, nobody initialed the narrow column for her thiamine tablet.  The supplement that was supposed to cover the loss went almost entirely ungiven, and the fish it was meant to cover happened to be the oldest fish in the building.

None of that amounts to a diagnosis, and the veterinarian was careful to say so twice.  It is simply a set of separate records that all point in the same direction, which is the most that a stack of paper can ever honestly do.

passages.title: Three Accounts of the Night Noise
passages.text:
Whitlock asked me to put all three accounts of the night noise onto a single page.  She wanted them in the witnesses' own words, as closely as I could manage, with nothing smoothed out.  Three people reported hearing something after closing on Wednesday evening, and no two of them described the same event.  A witness account is evidence, but it is a different kind of evidence than a log, and this page is where that difference starts to show.

The first account belongs to Cleo Fontaine, a visitor who was loading her car in the main lot.  She spoke to me by telephone on Thursday afternoon, a full day later, working entirely from memory.  Her words: it was a roar, exactly like a big cat, and it came from right beside the parking lot.  She placed the time at a little after eight o'clock, while she was folding a stroller into her trunk.  She said the sound was loud enough that she looked over her shoulder before getting into the car.

The second account belongs to Wes Tanaka, an evening volunteer who was closing the gift shop.  He wrote his account into the volunteer log the same night, roughly twenty minutes after he heard it.  His words: it came from the marsh, not the parking lot, and it was closer to nine than to eight.  He described the sound as somebody blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle, three times in a row, with a pause between each one.  He also wrote that it was low rather than loud, and that he felt it as much as he heard it.

The third account belongs to Ruth Bellweather, who lives across the creek from the marsh boardwalk.  She telephoned the office on Thursday morning without anybody asking her to, which is worth noting.  Her words: I have heard it on three separate evenings this week, always after dark, and always from the direction of the marsh.  She said it repeats like an old pump handle, and that her husband heard it on Monday as well.

Reading the three side by side, here is what they share and where they separate.  All three agree that the sound happened after closing and after dark.  Two of the three place it in the marsh, while one places it beside the parking lot.  Two of the three describe a low, repeating sound, while one describes a roar.  Only one account was written down the same night;  the other two were given from memory, one of them a full day afterward.  None of the three witnesses saw anything at all.

Whitlock's note at the bottom of my page is one sentence long.  Compare every account against the records before you compare it against another account.

passages.title: The Monitoring Summary, 41 Minutes
passages.text:
Marlowe Creek runs a sound recorder on a post at the marsh boardwalk from sunset until midnight.  A volunteer reviews the file the following morning.  The result is called the monitoring summary, and it fills one page for each night.  I pulled Wednesday's summary along with the gate log and the parking lot sheet, because those three records cover exactly the hours the witnesses described.

The summary begins with the amount of usable audio.  Wednesday's line reads: forty-one minutes usable out of four hours, the remainder lost to wind and highway noise.  Underneath that line the reviewer lists every sound he could identify, with the time of each one beside it.  The reviewer signs the bottom of every summary, and his initials appear on all three of this week's pages.

Between sunset and 8:40 p.m. the summary lists frogs, one distant siren, and a truck on the county road.  Nothing else appears anywhere in that stretch.  The first entry of interest comes later, and the reviewer wrote it out this way: low call, three occurrences, 9:04, 9:07, and 9:12, source not identified.  His final line recommends a field guide check rather than a guess.

The summary also carries a comparison box, because the reviewer had noticed something similar earlier in the week.  Monday's file lists the same unidentified low call at 9:16 p.m.  Tuesday's file lists it at 8:58 p.m.  Wednesday's entry is the third appearance of that call in the record in three consecutive nights.

The gate log is a separate sheet, signed by whoever closes the lot for the evening.  Wednesday's entry reads: last visitor vehicle out at 8:12 p.m., lot swept and empty at 8:20 p.m., chain across the lot entrance at 8:22 p.m.  Ola Sandoval signed all three of those lines.  A fourth line at the bottom of the sheet reads: no vehicle entered or left the lot after 8:22 p.m.

Laid beside the accounts, these records do two useful things and no more.  They give the low call a time.  That time falls some forty minutes after the parking lot was chained and empty.  They also show nothing whatsoever in the record during the hour one witness described.  The summary never names an animal, and it is not supposed to.  A monitoring summary records what was captured, not what it was.

passages.title: The Bittern's Boom
passages.text:
The sanctuary library keeps one battered regional field guide that every keeper here has used at some point.  Ferris handed it to me with his finger holding the marsh birds chapter and told me to read the entry aloud.  What follows is the entry itself, and then what Ferris said when I finished.

American bittern.  A member of the heron family and a bird of freshwater marshes, brown and tan and heavily streaked from throat to belly.  The guide's first note explains how the bird hides.  When a bittern believes it is being watched, it freezes with its bill pointed straight up.  The streaking on its throat lines up with the reeds around it until the bird effectively disappears.  The guide claims that patient observers have walked within a few feet of a standing bittern without ever seeing it.

The entry then describes the sound, and this is the paragraph Ferris wanted me to read.  The male's call is a low, pumping boom, written in older books as pump-er-lunk.  It is repeated in a short series with a pause between each one.  The guide calls the boom far deeper than most bird sounds and says it carries a surprising distance across open water.  It is given mostly in spring, and mostly at dusk or after dark.  The last sentence of the paragraph is the one I copied out twice: listeners who do not know the sound frequently assume it belongs to a much larger animal.

Ferris let me finish the whole entry before he said anything.  Then he pointed out the part that no field guide can tell you.  The animal inventory at Marlowe Creek lists no lions, no tigers, and nothing else on this property that roars.  The marsh is not an exhibit, he said;  it is a marsh, and wild birds arrive in it every spring without asking anybody's permission.

It is the second week of April.  The recorder has the low call at 9:16 on Monday, at 8:58 on Tuesday, and at 9:04 on Wednesday, always after dark and always from the marsh.  A bittern is a wild bird, so nobody can promise it will still be there tomorrow.  The case never required us to catch the bird, though.  It required us to stop treating the loudest description as the most reliable one.

passages.title: The Maintenance File on Fence Nine
passages.text:
Fence Nine is the woven-wire fence running along the north pasture, between the pasture and the creek.  It measures three hundred and forty feet end to end.  The maintenance binder gives every fence on the property its own section, and the section for Fence Nine is the thickest one in the book.  I copied out the last two months of it after the storm, together with the two work orders that follow.

The section opens with the inspection schedule, which is our own rule and nobody else's.  Every fence on the perimeter is walked end to end once every two weeks.  The keeper who walks it dates the line and initials it.  An inspection that was never initialed did not happen, as far as this binder is concerned.

The two most recent inspection lines read as follows.  On the twenty-eighth of April, Ray Bettencourt walked Fence Nine and tightened the mesh at panel six.  On the twelfth of May, Ray Bettencourt walked the same fence again and replaced two loose staples.  His line ends with the words all posts sound.

Work orders are kept separately from inspections, and this section contains two of them.  Work order 214, dated the third of April, covers the north service gate, whose hinge was rehung and whose latch pin was replaced.  Work order 318 was opened at 10:30 p.m. on the twenty-sixth of May, during the storm itself, and it reads: post fourteen snapped at ground level, mesh torn back on the creek side, temporary panel set, permanent repair to follow.

The discovery line is the one the newspaper never asked about.  It reads: gap in Fence Nine found during night rounds at 9:52 p.m. on the twenty-sixth of May by junior keeper Mara Delgado, reported by radio to Bo Ferris.  Underneath it, Bettencourt added a note the next morning.  A willow limb roughly fifteen feet long was lying across the fence line at post fourteen.  The break in the limb matches the big willow on the creek bank.

Every line in this section carries a date and a set of initials.  That is the entire point of keeping it.  A binder cannot tell you what actually happened out there in the dark.  It can tell you what somebody wrote down at the time, and who was willing to sign a name beside it.

passages.title: Bulletin 14: Wind Advisory
passages.text:
Bulletin 14 went up on the keeper room door at four o'clock on the afternoon of the twenty-sixth of May.  The operations desk posts a bulletin whenever weather is expected.  Every bulletin carries the same three parts.  What the weather service said comes first, what it means for this property comes second, and what each shift is expected to do comes last.

The first part is quoted directly, and the bulletin marks it clearly as a quotation.  The National Weather Service has issued a Wind Advisory for our county from 6 p.m. Thursday until 6 a.m. Friday.  West winds of 20 to 30 miles an hour are expected, with gusts of up to 50 miles an hour.

The second part is the operations desk explaining the first part in plain language.  A Wind Advisory covers conditions strong enough to make driving difficult and to bring branches down.  The bulletin reminds us that an advisory sits one step below a High Wind Warning, which the weather service issues when it expects worse.  We are under the advisory tonight, the bulletin says, and not under the warning.

The third part belongs entirely to us, and it takes the form of a list.  Bring the crane flock inside before dark.  Latch and pin every service gate, then check every pin a second time at 8 p.m. and initial the sheet beside the door.  Park the carts under the shed rather than beside the office.  Run rounds in pairs after dark, and carry two radios in case one of them fails.  Read the wind station on the maintenance shed at the top of every hour, and write the number down.

The bottom of the bulletin is a blank grid waiting for those hourly gust readings, and by morning the grid was full.  Seven o'clock came in at 24 miles an hour, eight o'clock at 31, and nine o'clock at 44.  The peak gust of the night is written in the margin beside the grid, 52 miles an hour at 9:20 p.m.  Every reading after ten o'clock falls steadily.  The operations desk checked with the weather service again before midnight, and the advisory it had quoted at four o'clock still stood, unchanged, through to six in the morning.  Those figures belong to our own wind station and our own evening keeper, and the bulletin never claims they are anybody else's.

The final line of Bulletin 14 is a sentence the operations desk prints on every single one of them.  A bulletin is not a forecast;  it is the record of what we did about a forecast.

passages.title: STORM RIPS SANCTUARY FENCE
passages.text:
The clipping ran in the Valley Register on the Saturday after the storm.  I taped it into the back of the maintenance binder because Whitlock asked me to.  She did not ask me to correct it.  She asked me to copy it out exactly and then read it beside our own records.  That turns out to be a different exercise.

The headline reads STORM RIPS SANCTUARY FENCE.  The byline belongs to a reporter named Cal Prentiss.  The article opens this way.  A violent spring storm tore a hole in the perimeter fence at Marlowe Creek Wildlife Sanctuary Thursday night, leaving a gap wide enough for an animal to walk through.

Several details in the article are perfectly accurate.  A post did snap at ground level, a temporary panel was set the same night, and no animal left the property.  The article also quotes Head Keeper Whitlock correctly, in a single line: every animal was accounted for by eleven o'clock, and the fence was closed before midnight.

Two of the article's claims do not survive a comparison with our own paperwork.  The first is a sentence about upkeep: sanctuary records show the fence had not been inspected since March.  The second is a sentence about the weather: the county was under a High Wind Warning that night, according to the National Weather Service.  Both sentences are printed as plain statements of fact.  The first points at records nobody outside this building can open.  The second names the weather service without naming the product it issued.

The remainder of the article rests on a single unnamed source, described only as a neighbor who asked not to be identified.  That neighbor is quoted saying the sanctuary had been warned about that fence for years.  Prentiss never asked to see the maintenance binder.  Nobody here was asked about the inspection schedule at all.

A newspaper is a source like any other source.  It can be checked in exactly the way we check our own paperwork.  The difference in this case is that our binder names the keeper who walked the fence and the date he walked it, while the article names nobody whatsoever.

passages.title: The Long Way Down the Sky
passages.text:
She had flown that line down the valley more times than she could have counted, if counting were a thing she did.  The river supplied the direction and the cottonwoods supplied the edges, and the changing light told her when to travel.  All afternoon the air had been a road underneath her.

By evening the road was gone, and the storm had pulled the light down long before the sun was due to follow it.  The wind arrived from the wrong side of the sky, in shoves rather than in gusts, and every shove moved her farther from the water she had aimed at.  She did exactly what her body already understood.  She folded her neck back against her shoulders, trailed her legs out straight behind her, and beat down hard into air that kept sliding out from underneath her.

A heron is assembled for patience rather than for speed.  Her wings are enormous and unhurried, designed for carrying her considerable distances without any effort.  The wind that evening carried no patience anywhere inside it.  It discovered the entire broad surface of her and pushed, and the pushing never stopped.

The valley she knew slid sideways out of view.  Below her the ground became a collection of shapes she remembered nothing about: a roadway curving the wrong direction, a rooftop, a field of low brush.  A line of small cold lights came up out of the dark, strung in a row like something a person had decided on.  Beyond the lights lay water, black and wrinkling, and water is the one thing she can always read.

She came down toward it too fast, and she came down crooked.  The last of the wind caught her at the moment she had nothing left to answer it with.  Something long and thin went past her in the dark, a branch or a wire, and her left wing took the whole of it.  The wing came down.  It never came back up the way the other one did.

Reeds broke her landing, which was the only kindness the evening offered her.  She stood in eight inches of cold water with the rain arriving sideways and did not move for a long time.  Standing still is not a decision for her;  standing still is what she is.  A heron out in the open holds still until stillness stops working.

The rain continued without interruption.  The wind pulled at the reeds surrounding her and produced a sound like the entire marsh breathing at once.  She could feel her wing as a heaviness that would not fold in and would not lift.

Eventually a light came along the boardwalk, low and yellow, swinging with somebody's footsteps.  The light stopped where the boardwalk ended.  She pointed her bill straight at the sky and held so still that even her eyes stopped moving, because stillness is what she possesses instead of running.  The light stayed where it was, at a distance.  After a while a voice traveled out into the darkness, low and steady, and it never came any closer.

passages.title: The Rehabber's Van
passages.text:
Thursday, 7:15 in the evening, under a sky the storm had already turned the colour of slate, and the wind was loud enough that I had to key my radio twice.

I found her from the boardwalk, thirty feet out in the shallow water, standing exactly where no heron in her right mind stands during a storm.  Great blue heron, adult, one wing carried wrong.  She had her bill pointed straight up when my light reached her, a posture I have since read about in bitterns, and which our field guide says herons will also take when they hold still.

Here is what I did not do.  I never waded out to her, I never threw a towel over her, and I never attempted to carry her anywhere at all.  Whitlock's rule about wild animals is one sentence long, and every keeper here can recite it from memory.  A wild animal that lands on our property is not our animal.

We are not licensed to treat wild birds.  The sanctuary cares for the residents in its files and for nobody else, and a heron off the river belongs to a different set of rules than Rana does.  My job was to keep my distance, keep her in sight, and get somebody on the telephone whose license covers exactly this.

That somebody is Alva Reyes, a licensed wildlife rehabilitator who lives forty minutes from here and has taken birds from us before.  Whitlock reached her by telephone at 7:22.  Alva asked four questions, and not one of them was a question I had expected.  Was the bird standing, and was it standing in water.  How close had anybody approached it, and how long ago.

Then she said she was on her way, and she added one more thing that I wrote down word for word.  Do not chase her.  A bird that runs from you in a storm is a bird with a second injury.

Her van pulled up to the maintenance gate a little after eight, in rain that was coming down flat.  She works quietly, and she arrived carrying a towel, a crate lined with something soft, and a way of moving that made her appear considerably slower than she actually was.  She came at the heron from the side rather than the front, talking the whole time in a low voice that had nothing to do with words.  It took her under a minute.  The bill goes into the towel first, which she told me afterward is the part nobody forgets, because a heron's bill is a spear and it is aimed at your face.

At the van she filled out a transfer slip on the hood, in the rain, with the crate already loaded, and the time she wrote on it was 8:40.  Time, place, species, condition, the name of the keeper who found the bird, and both signatures.  Whitlock signed it and Alva signed it, and I carried the carbon copy back to the maintenance binder.

That slip is the last thing our file will ever say about this bird.  She is not our animal, and I know perfectly well that this is the correct answer.  I stood at the gate anyway, in the wind, until the taillights were gone.

passages.title: The Bird We Did Not Name
passages.text:
Every animal in our files has a name, and the names are not decoration.  Juniper's name sits at the top of a page holding four years of her weights, her burrow map, and the note that told a panicking new keeper where to look.  A name is the anchor that an entire record hangs from.

The heron never got a name.  I asked Ferris about that on Saturday, and he took long enough answering that I recognized the question was a genuine one.  A resident gets a name, he said, because a resident has a history with us and will have more of it tomorrow.  A wild bird passing through gets a date, a species, and a set of initials.

I told him the practice sounded cold, and he admitted it had sounded cold to him as well, for about a year.  Then he explained the part I had not thought about at all.  The moment you name a wild animal, you begin telling a story about her, and the story quietly manufactures the parts you do not actually know.  You decide that she was brave.  You decide that she was heading home.  You decide she will be back in the spring, standing in those same reeds, and you write that in your head instead of writing down what you actually saw.

He is correct, and I thoroughly dislike how correct he is.  I had already invented half a story about her on the walk back from the gate.

There is a second reason, and Whitlock gave me that one on Monday.  Our files go to other people.  A transfer slip goes to a rehabilitator, an inspection line goes to an inspector, and a monitoring summary goes to whoever asks for it.  A record that says adult great blue heron, left wing, found at 7:15 p.m. means the same thing to every one of those readers.  A record that says Willow means whatever the reader would like it to mean.

So the bird has no name in our binder.  There is one line about her in the daily log, and there is a carbon copy of a slip that somebody else signed, and that is the whole of it.

I looked out at the marsh on my last round tonight, the way I have every night this week.  The water was flat, the frogs were noisy, and absolutely nothing was standing in the shallows.  I do not know how she is.  Alva is not required to tell us, and we are not entitled to ask her.

What I keep coming back to is that refusing to name her is a kind of respect.  It is the hardest kind, because from the outside it looks exactly like not caring.

passages.title: The Night of the Storm: What the Records Show
passages.text:
Whitlock's assignment after the storm was a single sentence.  Build one page that puts every record of the night of the twenty-sixth of May in order, and mark every place where they disagree.

Five records cover that night, and one recollection does not.  The five are the gate log, the radio log, the wind station grid at the bottom of Bulletin 14, work order 318, and the signed transfer slip for the heron.  The recollection belongs to Wes Tanaka, who was on the property until nine and wrote nothing down.

The evening begins on paper at four o'clock, when Bulletin 14 went up on the keeper room door.  The advisory it quotes began at 6 p.m.  The radio log's first entry that matters comes at 7:15 p.m., when I reported a great blue heron down in the marsh with one wing carried wrong.  The gate log shows the last visitor vehicle out at 7:40 p.m., and the pedestrian gate pinned and initialed at 7:44 p.m.  The radio log also records Ferris sending every keeper out in pairs at 8:05 p.m., exactly as the bulletin asked.

Bulletin 14 requires a second check of every service gate pin at 8 p.m., initialed on the sheet beside the keeper room door.  The sheet for the twenty-sixth of May has a printed line for eight o'clock and nothing written on it.  No initials appear anywhere in that row.

The transfer slip is signed at 8:40 p.m., at the maintenance gate, by Head Keeper Whitlock and by the licensed rehabilitator who took the bird.  Tanaka remembers that van differently.  He told me the van left while there was still light in the sky, before the wind picked up, maybe seven-thirty.  The slip carries a time and two signatures, while his memory carries neither, and he is the first person to say so.

The wind station grid runs alongside all of this.  Nine o'clock reads 44 miles an hour, and the margin records the night's peak gust, 52 miles an hour at 9:20 p.m.

The radio log then carries the two entries that the rest of the file turns on.  At 9:52 p.m. I reported the gap in Fence Nine at post fourteen.  At 10:05 p.m. Ferris reported the north service gate standing open, with its latch pin lying in the mud below the hinge, bent.

Work order 318 opens at 10:30 p.m. and closes the fence with a temporary panel.  The radio log's final entry of the night comes at 10:56 p.m.: all animals accounted for, count closed, no animal off property.

Here is what this page can settle.  It can settle when the gap was found and who found it, because two separate records agree.  It can settle that the heron left with a licensed rehabilitator at 8:40 p.m., because a signed slip outweighs a memory.  It can settle that the eight o'clock pin check was never initialed, because the line for it is empty.

Here is what this page cannot settle.  It cannot say how the pin came out of that gate, because no record was written while it was happening and nobody saw it.  A timeline is not a witness.  It shows which questions are answered, and it shows exactly where the answers stop.

passages.title: The Morning Report
passages.text:
Whitlock files a morning report after any night that produces a work order.  This one ran to two full pages.  I am copying out the argument rather than the whole document, because the argument is the part that will still matter in a month.

The report opens with findings, and it keeps them separate from everything else on purpose.  Finding one: a willow limb came down across Fence Nine at post fourteen, and the post snapped at ground level.  The gap was found on rounds at 9:52 p.m. and closed with a temporary panel before eleven.  Finding two: the north service gate was found standing open at 10:05 p.m., and the eight o'clock pin check required by Bulletin 14 was never initialed.  The report says nothing whatsoever about how the pin came out, which is the sentence I would have been most tempted to write.

Then the report makes an argument, and it makes that argument in three steps.

The first step is that the fence failure was not a failure of upkeep.  The report supports that step with the inspection line dated the twelfth of May, initialed by the keeper who walked the fence.  The second step is that the open gate was a failure of procedure, whatever the equipment did.  The report supports that step with the blank eight o'clock line rather than with anybody's opinion.  The third step ties the whole stack of paper together.  The sanctuary's defense is not that nothing went wrong, because something plainly did.  The defense is that everything which went wrong was written down by the people it went wrong for.

Three changes follow from those steps, and each change names the record it repairs.  The pin check gains a second initial column, exactly like the supplement column on a diet card.  One signature can no longer cover two separate jobs.  The wind station grid gets filled in by whoever is walking rounds, rather than by whoever remembers at the end of the night.  The volunteer log gains a new line at the top of every entry, asking what you heard and when you wrote it down.

The last section is a letter, and Whitlock attached a copy of it.  The letter asks the Valley Register for a correction.  It names two claims, along with the record that contradicts each one.  Against the sentence about no inspection since March, it cites the inspection line from the twelfth of May.  Against the sentence about a High Wind Warning, it cites Bulletin 14, which quotes a Wind Advisory and explains the difference between the two.  The letter asks for nothing else.  It does not argue about the headline, and it never complains about the unnamed neighbor.

The report ends with a line I fully intend to steal.  A record is not a defense of the person who wrote it.  It is a promise to the person who reads it next.

levels.name: First Rounds
levels.goal: Walk the evening route, and learn why a keeper writes down what she sees.

levels.name: The Wrong Diet
levels.goal: Read a diet card, a vet memo, and an invoice until the otter's slow week makes sense.

levels.name: The Night Noise
levels.goal: Weigh three witness accounts against the night's own records.

levels.name: The Heron's Night

partA.stem: Why does the narrator write down two on her sheet, even though she wants to write down three?
choices: Because two is the number she actually counted, and her instructions are to record what she observes.
Because writing three would have kept her at the sanctuary later than she wanted to stay.
Because the gate log will not accept any count until a keeper signs for it.
Because she had counted only once and did not trust a single pass through the yard.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The gate log at the bottom of the hill wanted a signature and a time, and I stood there holding the pen without signing anything.
Count everything twice, she said, and record what you actually observe, never what you expect to observe.
I counted a second time, exactly the way she had instructed me, and arrived at two again.
Every part of me wanted to write down three, because three was the comfortable number that would have let me go home.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says the opposite: three was the number that would have let her go home, so writing it would have ended her night sooner, not later.
distractorRationale.2: The gate log did want a signature, but what stops her is the number itself, not a rule about when the log can be filled in.
distractorRationale.3: She counted twice, exactly the way she had been instructed, and reached two both times, so an untrusted single count is not the reason.

items.explain: Whitlock's rule is to record what you actually observe rather than what you expect, and two is what the narrator observed on both counts.  The wrong choices each borrow a real detail from the night, the log, the wish to go home, the second count, and treat it as the reason she hesitated.

partA.stem: What does the narrator notice at the otter pool during her first night alone?
choices: Something large moved through the water beside the otter pool without being seen.
Rana met her at the glass with flattened whiskers, exactly as she always does.
Rana did not come to the glass the way she normally does.
The detail was too small to be worth writing on the sheet at all.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: After the foxes comes the otter pool, where Rana ordinarily meets me at the glass with her whiskers flattened against it.
I almost failed to write that down, because at the time it seemed like nothing worth recording.
Something large moved through the reeds while I was standing there, slowly and completely unbothered, and I never did see what it was.
She did not meet me this evening.

distractorRationale.0: The large animal moved through the reeds out in the marsh, farther along the route, and the passage never places it at the otter pool.
distractorRationale.1: That sentence describes what Rana ordinarily does on other evenings, which is the very thing the next sentence says did not happen tonight.
distractorRationale.3: She almost skipped it for exactly that reason, and then wrote it down anyway, which is the whole point of the entry.

items.explain: The entry records an absence: Rana, who usually meets the narrator at the glass, did not appear at all that evening.  Two wrong choices lift real sentences about the otter's usual habit or the narrator's hesitation, and one moves the marsh animal to the wrong stop on the route.

partA.stem: Which idea does the narrator settle on by the end of her first night alone?
choices: Evening rounds work best when they are always walked in the same order.
A record is only useful later if it was honest when somebody wrote it.
A keeper should write down whichever number lets the paperwork close.
The tortoise yard is the most difficult stop on the whole route.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: Whitlock believes the tortoise yard teaches a new keeper more than any other stop on the route, because nothing inside it ever happens quickly.
Every part of me wanted to write down three, because three was the comfortable number that would have let me go home.
The sheet is a record, and a record can only help somebody later if it was honest at the moment somebody wrote it.
Evening rounds begin at the top of the hill and work downward toward the creek.

distractorRationale.0: The order of the route is background about how rounds work, not the lesson the narrator draws at the end of the entry.
distractorRationale.2: That is the temptation she describes and then refuses;  the passage treats the comfortable number as the wrong answer, not the lesson.
distractorRationale.3: Whitlock says the yard teaches a keeper the most, which is a claim about learning rather than about difficulty.

items.explain: The closing lines separate a wish from a record and land on honesty at the moment of writing as the thing that makes a record worth anything.  Each wrong choice restates a true detail from earlier in the entry and mistakes it for the point the narrator is actually making.

partA.stem: What does Ferris tell the narrator to do with her count when he answers the radio?
choices: Climb the wall and check the far side of the enclosure before he arrives.
Assume she miscounted, the way new keepers usually do on a first night.
Bring him the count she actually got, without fixing or improving it.
Search the enclosure in a slow grid by herself before he gets there.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: He promised to meet me at the tortoise yard with the yard binder, and he told me not to climb the wall or start digging anywhere.
We searched the enclosure in a slow grid, shoulder to shoulder, with our hands out of our pockets.
Do not fix the number, he said, and do not improve it either.
He never once suggested that I had simply miscounted, which I appreciated more than he knows.

distractorRationale.0: He instructs her to do the opposite, telling her not to climb the wall and not to start digging while she waits.
distractorRationale.1: The narrator specifically notes that he never suggested she had miscounted, which is why the call meant so much to her.
distractorRationale.3: The grid search does happen, but only once Ferris is standing beside her;  it is not part of what he tells her to do over the radio.

items.explain: Ferris asks for the raw number, unfixed and unimproved, which is the same discipline Whitlock taught with her counting rule.  The wrong choices each swap in something he explicitly ruled out or something he said about the search rather than about the number.

partA.stem: According to the yard binder, why is Juniper missing from the evening count?
choices: She has dug herself a burrow and gone underground, which she has done before.
An earlier keeper moved her to a different part of the yard.
The count sheet was printed with the wrong number of tortoises on it.
She is under the feeding shelf, where the sand stays warmer than the air.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Warmer than the air out here, he reported.
Then she took my clipboard, wrote down the number two, and beside it recorded a full line about the burrow, the time, and the keeper who had checked it.
During her first autumn at the sanctuary she went under the east slope and remained underground for nineteen days, and every keeper on the evening shift aged a decade.
Underneath that entry, in a different color of ink, somebody had drawn a careful little map.

distractorRationale.1: No entry describes a move at all;  the map marks a burrow Juniper dug herself, which is the opposite of somebody relocating her.
distractorRationale.2: Nothing in the binder questions the sheet, and Whitlock corrects the count rather than the form, so a printing error is invented.
distractorRationale.3: Ferris feels the warmer air at the burrow mouth behind the manzanita;  the feeding shelf is where Ada was found, not Juniper.

items.explain: A four-year-old entry records that Juniper digs and once stayed under for nineteen days, which turns a frightening gap in the count into a known habit.  The wrong choices invent a move, a printing error, or a hiding place that the binder and the search both rule out.

partA.stem: What does Whitlock mean when she says a count that refuses to close is not a failure?
choices: It means nobody can be blamed when an animal cannot be found.
It means the keeper should keep searching until the numbers finally match.
It means an open count should be closed with the number everyone expected.
It means an open count is a question written down well enough for the next keeper to answer.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: The count still would not close, and Whitlock told me that was perfectly fine.
A count that refuses to close is not a failure, she explained.
It is a question you have written down carefully enough that the next keeper can actually answer it.
Then she took my clipboard, wrote down the number two, and beside it recorded a full line about the burrow, the time, and the keeper who had checked it.

distractorRationale.0: Blame never enters her explanation;  her point is about what an open record does for the keeper who reads it next.
distractorRationale.1: She ends the search once the burrow is found and calls the open count fine, so continued searching is not what she is asking for.
distractorRationale.2: She writes the observed number and adds an explanation beside it, which is the opposite of closing the count with the expected three.

items.explain: Whitlock reframes an unfinished count as a question passed forward in usable shape, which is why she records the burrow, the time, and the checker beside the number.  Each wrong choice treats the open count as a problem to erase, to excuse, or to keep searching until it disappears.

partA.stem: Why is the tortoise in this passage staying underground?
choices: Something frightened her near the tunnel mouth and she is waiting it out.
Her body is settling into a long, deliberate stillness for the cold months.
She is ill, since she has stopped eating and her heartbeat has slowed.
The burrow is where her food is stored for the cold part of the year.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: Now food had stopped interesting her entirely.
Her body had already begun putting itself away for the cold months ahead.
She had eaten generously through the green weeks, the grasses and the weeds and the flat pads she had to work at patiently.
Once, something dragged for a long time near the mouth of the tunnel, and she drew her head back and waited until the dragging went away.

distractorRationale.0: She does pull her head back when something drags past, but the passage rules out fear as the reason she went under in the first place.
distractorRationale.2: The passage states plainly that nothing hurt and nothing was wrong;  the slowing is what the season does to her, not a sign of sickness.
distractorRationale.3: No food is described underground anywhere;  she ate through the green weeks first and then lost interest in eating altogether.

items.explain: The passage describes a body preparing itself for cold: eating stops, the heart slows, and the stillness is deliberate rather than forced.  The wrong choices read the same slowing as fear, as illness, or as a food store, all of which the text contradicts within a few sentences.

partA.stem: What difference does the passage draw between hiding and what the tortoise is actually doing?
choices: Hiding happens quickly, while digging her burrow took her an entire morning.
Hiding happens above ground, while she has taken herself below it.
Hiding is a response to something, while this is a season she is entering.
Hiding is silent, while she can still feel feet and carts moving overhead.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: They are flat and scaled and built for moving ground, and they moved ground steadily all morning.
She could still feel the world arriving through the floor.
The hole became a tunnel that bent once and took away the last of the sky.
This was a season instead, and she was going down into it the way water goes downhill.

distractorRationale.0: The morning of digging is real, but the passage separates hiding from a season by what causes each one, not by how long it takes.
distractorRationale.1: Where she is does not settle the question;  the passage defines hiding by the thing an animal is hiding from, and nothing is after her.
distractorRationale.3: Feeling the world through the floor shows how much still reaches her underground, not what makes her stillness different from hiding.

items.explain: The passage defines hiding as something an animal does about a threat, then says this is a season instead, entered the way water goes downhill.  The wrong choices measure the difference by speed, by depth, or by noise, none of which is the distinction the sentence actually draws.

items.stem: Choose the three things the yard binder actually records about Juniper.
choices: A note saying that Juniper digs and has always dug.
A count sheet showing three tortoises living in the yard.
A map marking the mouth of a burrow behind the manzanita.
A warning in capital letters not to dig her out.
The date she is expected to come back to the surface.

distractorRationale.1: The count sheet is the narrator's own clipboard from evening rounds, not an entry inside the binder's tortoise section.
distractorRationale.4: Whitlock says plainly that nobody can tell you how long Juniper will stay under, so no return date exists anywhere in the binder.

items.explain: The binder holds a four-year-old note about her digging, a hand-drawn map of the burrow mouth, and a capitalized warning against digging her out.  The two wrong choices move the narrator's clipboard into the binder and invent a return date the passage explicitly refuses to give.

items.stem: Select the three details this passage gives about the burrow and about the tortoise's body.
choices: The air inside stays cool and slightly damp whether the sun is up or gone.
Her heart and breathing slow until her sides barely appear to move.
The tunnel runs straight, so she can still see the sky from the bottom.
She stopped being interested in food after eating through the green weeks.
She keeps a store of food underground to last her through the cold.

distractorRationale.2: The tunnel bends once, and the passage says that bend took away the last of the sky, so no view remains from the bottom.
distractorRationale.4: No food appears underground at all;  the passage says food had simply stopped interesting her once the green weeks ended.

items.explain: The burrow holds air that stays cool and damp no matter what the surface does, and her body answers by slowing her heart, her breathing, and her appetite.  The two wrong choices add a straight tunnel and a food store, both of which the passage rules out directly.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the rule the narrator is given and the reason she decides it matters.
spans: Count everything twice, she said, and record what you actually observe, never what you expect to observe.
The sheet is a record, and a record can only help somebody later if it was honest at the moment somebody wrote it.
Evening rounds begin at the top of the hill and work downward toward the creek.
The barn owls come first, because they are awake and impatient before anything else in the sanctuary stirs.
Their names are Juniper, Ada, and Salt.
items.explain: The rule arrives in Whitlock's own words at the start, record what you observe rather than what you expect, and the closing line supplies the reason: a record is only useful later if it was honest when written.  The other three sentences describe the route and the animals on it, which is background rather than the entry's point.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that report where a tortoise was actually found during the search.
spans: Ada was underneath the feeding shelf, half buried in sand that still held the afternoon's warmth.
Salt was pressed against the north wall with her head tucked completely inside her shell.
Juniper was nowhere at all.
We searched the enclosure in a slow grid, shoulder to shoulder, with our hands out of our pockets.
Ferris ran his flashlight along the base of the slope and said nothing whatsoever for a long while.
items.explain: Only two sentences put a tortoise in a specific place: Ada under the feeding shelf and Salt against the north wall.  Juniper being nowhere is the absence that starts the case rather than a location, and the other two describe how the keepers searched instead of what they found.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that report what the yard binder itself says about Juniper.
spans: Juniper digs, the note said, and Juniper has always dug.
During her first autumn at the sanctuary she went under the east slope and remained underground for nineteen days, and every keeper on the evening shift aged a decade.
It estimated the depth in feet, and it said, in capital letters, DO NOT DIG HER OUT.
The manzanita had grown out across the sand in the years since the map was drawn.
Warmer than the air out here, he reported.
items.explain: Three sentences carry the binder's own content: the note that Juniper digs, the record of nineteen days underground, and the map with its depth and its capitalised warning.  The overgrown manzanita and the warmth at the burrow mouth are things the keepers observe at the yard that night, not entries anybody wrote in the binder.

items.stem: Tap the three phrases showing that the tortoise is going into a season rather than reacting to something.  The other two describe a moment when something did disturb her.
spans: putting itself away for the cold months ahead
food had stopped interesting her entirely
becoming extremely still, on purpose
drew her head back and waited
hiding is a thing an animal does about something
items.explain: A body putting itself away, an appetite that has switched off, and stillness described as deliberate all belong to the season the passage says she is entering.  Drawing her head back is her one reaction to a disturbance, and the definition of hiding is the idea the passage raises in order to rule it out.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The narrator writes down two because {{0}}, even though {{1}}.

choices: the gate log refuses to accept a three
two is the number she actually counted, both times
she has decided that a tortoise escaped over the wall
part of her wants the comfortable three that would let her go home
Whitlock told her to record the number she expected
the yard binder had already explained where Juniper was

items.explain: She counted twice and got two both times, and her instructions are to record what she observed rather than what she expected, so two is what goes on the sheet.  The pull she has to resist is the comfortable three, the number that would have closed the count and let her leave.  The gate log never refuses a number, she never concludes a tortoise escaped, and the binder does not explain anything until Whitlock opens it later that night.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The count will not close because {{0}}, and Whitlock treats an open count as {{1}}.

choices: a keeper miscounted the tortoise yard in the dark
one tortoise was moved without anybody writing it down
Juniper has dug herself in, exactly as the binder says she does
a mistake that has to be corrected before anybody goes home
a question recorded well enough for the next keeper to answer
proof that nobody on the evening shift is to blame

items.explain: The binder settles the gap: Juniper digs, she has stayed under for nineteen days before, and the map marks the burrow she is in now.  Whitlock therefore writes two and adds the burrow, the time, and the checker beside it, calling the open count a question passed forward rather than a failure.  Nobody miscounted, nobody moved a tortoise, and her point is about what the record does next rather than about who is to blame.

items.stem: What does Whitlock's counting rule actually ask a keeper to do?
choices: Write down what she sees, even when it disagrees with the sheet
Count until the yard and the sheet finally agree
Count once quickly, then move on to the next stop
Ask a senior keeper before recording any unusual number

distractorRationale.1: This treats agreement as the goal, but the whole entry turns on a count that never agrees and gets written down anyway.
distractorRationale.2: The rule asks for two counts, and the narrator gets the same answer twice before she writes anything.
distractorRationale.3: She does radio Ferris, but only after she has already written the number she observed;  the rule is about the writing, not about permission.

items.explain: The rule separates observation from expectation: count twice, then record what you actually saw.  Its whole point is the case where those two things differ, which is exactly the night this entry describes.

items.stem: Why do the barn owls come first on the evening route?
choices: Their enclosure sits closest to the sanctuary gate
They are already awake and impatient before the rest of the sanctuary stirs
They are the animals most likely to be missing from a count
They have to be fed before the foxes will settle

distractorRationale.0: The route ends near the gate at the tortoise yard;  the owls are at the top of the hill, where rounds begin.
distractorRationale.2: The count that fails is in the tortoise yard, and nothing suggests the owls are ever hard to account for.
distractorRationale.3: The foxes wait for their own bowl, and no feeding order links the two enclosures.

items.explain: The route follows the animals' own clocks rather than the map: owls wake earliest, so they are visited first, and the foxes who pretend to sleep come next.  Position on the hill and the risk of a miscount belong to other parts of the entry.

items.stem: What does the narrator most appreciate about how Ferris answers her radio call?
choices: He tells her the tortoise is certainly safe underground
He offers to finish her rounds so she can go home
He never suggests that a new keeper simply counted wrong
He agrees to leave the number off the sheet until morning

distractorRationale.0: Nobody knows that yet;  the burrow is not found until Whitlock arrives with the binder.
distractorRationale.1: He asks her to wait at the yard, and she stays for the whole search.
distractorRationale.3: His instruction is the opposite: bring the number she actually got, unfixed and unimproved.

items.explain: Taking a new keeper's count seriously is what makes the rest of the night possible, and the narrator notices it immediately.  Each wrong choice offers a comfort he never gives: certainty, an early night, or a delay in writing the number down.

items.stem: Why does nobody dig the burrow open once it is found?
choices: The sand is packed too hard for the keepers to dig through
Digging would violate a rule written by the state inspector
They cannot be certain which burrow she went into
How long she stays under is her business rather than the keepers'

distractorRationale.0: Nobody tries and nobody says it would be difficult;  the reason given is about the animal, not the ground.
distractorRationale.1: The warning the keepers actually follow is in the sanctuary's own yard binder, in a keeper's handwriting;  no outside inspector is mentioned anywhere in the entry.
distractorRationale.2: The map marks the burrow behind the manzanita, and Ferris confirms the warm air at its mouth.

items.explain: The binder's capitalised warning and Whitlock's answer agree: a brumating tortoise is left alone, and nobody can say when she will surface.  The wrong choices invent a physical obstacle, an outside rule, or a doubt the map and the warm air have already settled.

items.stem: What still reaches the tortoise once the tunnel bends?
choices: Movement overhead, carried to her through the ground itself
Daylight, which reaches all the way to where she rests
The changing temperature of the day above her
The smell of the food she has stopped eating

distractorRationale.1: Light reaches the bend of the tunnel and no further;  the passage says it never once reaches her.
distractorRationale.2: The burrow holds its own cool, damp air whatever the surface does, which is described as its first gift.
distractorRationale.3: Food has simply stopped interesting her, and no scent from the surface appears anywhere in the passage.

items.explain: Feet and a cart arrive as vibration through the floor of the burrow, which is the one channel the passage leaves open to her.  Light, temperature swings, and food are each named specifically as things the burrow shuts out.

items.stem: The passage compares her going under to water running downhill.  What does that comparison suggest?
choices: She moves quickly once she has started digging
She is following something settled and unforced, not making a decision
She is being pushed into the burrow by the cold
She will come back up as soon as the weather turns

distractorRationale.0: Speed is not the point of the image;  the passage stresses slowing down, and the digging takes a whole morning.
distractorRationale.2: Cold is the season she goes into rather than a force shoving her;  the wanting to dig arrives before the cold does.
distractorRationale.3: The passage refuses to say when she surfaces, and Whitlock says plainly that nobody can tell you.

items.explain: Water downhill is the image the passage picks precisely because nothing chooses it and nothing forces it;  it simply follows the shape of things.  The comparison is about the absence of decision, not about speed, pressure, or a return date.

items.stem: Match each thing the keepers find to what it actually tells them.
rowLabels: Sand under the feeding shelf still holding the afternoon's warmth
A four-year-old note about nineteen days underground
Air at the burrow mouth warmer than the air outside
colLabels: Juniper has done this before, so the gap in the count has a precedent
A tortoise is down there right now
Ada settled where the sand still held the afternoon's warmth
items.explain: Each find answers a different question: the warm sand explains where Ada settled, the old note supplies a precedent for a tortoise vanishing from a count, and the warm air at the burrow mouth is present-tense evidence that somebody is inside.  Collapsing them into one clue loses the difference between history and a live reading.

items.stem: Match each line from the narrator's first night to what it is doing in the entry.
rowLabels: Count everything twice, and record what you observe
Three desert tortoises live there on a slope of packed sand
The sheet is not a wish
colLabels: Naming the lesson the whole night has been building toward
Stating the rule the narrator is handed at six o'clock
Setting the scene the count will later fail in
items.explain: The entry has three jobs and one line for each: a rule handed over at the start, a setting described so the failure means something, and a conclusion drawn at the end.  Reading all three as background detail is what makes the closing lines feel like they arrive from nowhere.

partA.stem: What does the narrator find when she reads down the narrow supplement column for the past two weeks?
choices: Every one of the twenty-eight feeds was initialed in both columns.
The supplement was initialed on only three of the fourteen days.
The column is meant for the fish, so blanks in it do not matter.
The supplement is optional on days when the fish is freshly delivered.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Thiamine supplement, one tablet, crushed into the first feed, daily, no exceptions.
The supplement column beside them carries initials on three days.
Fourteen days of feeding produced twenty-eight fish squares, and every one of them was initialed.
That narrow column is only for the supplement.

distractorRationale.0: The twenty-eight initials are in the fish grid;  the narrow column beside that grid is the one that is nearly empty.
distractorRationale.2: The card reserves that narrow column entirely for the supplement, which is exactly why blanks in it are the thing to notice.
distractorRationale.3: The card sets the tablet apart in its own box and marks it daily with no exceptions, so no version of it is optional.

items.explain: Fourteen days produced twenty-eight initialed fish squares and only three initials in the supplement column beside them.  The wrong choices move the fish grid's initials into the narrow column, dismiss the column as unimportant, or invent a freshness exception the card explicitly denies.

partA.stem: Why does the diet card ask for a second initial in a column of its own?
choices: Because two keepers have to be present at every scheduled feeding.
Because the tablet is given at a different time of day than the fish.
Because the front freezer requires a signature line of its own.
Because a single initial lets a keeper remember the fish and forget the tablet.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: Thiamine supplement, one tablet, crushed into the first feed, daily, no exceptions.
It reads: fish drawn from front freezer only, oldest lot first, blue tag before white tag.
Whitlock says a single initial lets a person remember the fish and forget the tablet.
It is a grid of small squares, one square for every feed, and a keeper initials the square once the feeding is done.

distractorRationale.0: The second initial covers a second task rather than a second person;  nothing on the card requires two keepers at a feeding.
distractorRationale.1: The tablet is crushed into the first feed itself, so the extra initial is not marking a separate feeding time.
distractorRationale.2: Freezer rules live in the card's third block;  the narrow initial column belongs to the supplement and to nothing else.

items.explain: The card splits the initials because the two jobs fail separately: fish gets remembered, and a crushed tablet does not.  Each wrong choice explains the second column with a rule about people, timing, or freezers rather than with the failure the design is actually built to catch.

partA.stem: What does a white tag on a lot of fish mean, according to the diet card?
choices: The lot belongs in the front freezer and should be thawed first.
The lot was packed during the current season.
The lot has been held much longer and must be pulled and checked before thawing.
The lot has already been inspected and cleared for use.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: A white tag marks a lot held much longer, and any white-tag lot must be pulled and checked by a keeper before anybody thaws it.
It reads: fish drawn from front freezer only, oldest lot first, blue tag before white tag.
A blue tag marks a lot packed during the current season.
Beneath that instruction, in smaller type, the card explains what the two tags mean.

distractorRationale.0: The card puts blue tags ahead of white ones in the thawing order, so a white tag is not the lot to reach for first.
distractorRationale.1: That is what a blue tag marks;  the white tag is the older category the card surrounds with extra caution.
distractorRationale.3: The checking is what still has to happen;  a white tag is an instruction to inspect, not a record that somebody already did.

items.explain: The card defines a white tag as an older lot that a keeper must pull and check before anybody thaws it, in contrast to a blue tag from the current season.  The wrong choices swap the two tags, reverse the thawing order, or read an instruction as a completed inspection.

partA.stem: According to the memo, what does the enzyme thiaminase actually do?
choices: It breaks thiamine apart, which is the vitamin the animal needs for energy.
It preserves fish for as long as the fish stays frozen.
It replaces the thiamine that a frozen diet is missing.
It causes fever and swelling in animals fed a raw fish diet.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: Freezing slows that enzyme down considerably, but freezing does not destroy it.
Her eyes, ears, teeth, and coat all look normal, and she has no fever, no wound, and no swelling anywhere.
The supplement exists to replace what the enzyme removes.
Many kinds of fish carry thiaminase naturally, and the enzyme does exactly one thing: it breaks thiamine apart.

distractorRationale.1: Freezing is what slows the enzyme;  the enzyme preserves nothing and keeps working the entire time the fish sits in the freezer.
distractorRationale.2: Replacing the loss is the supplement's job;  the enzyme is the reason a supplement is needed in the first place.
distractorRationale.3: The examination found no fever and no swelling at all, and the signs the memo watches for are slowness and appetite loss.

items.explain: The memo gives thiaminase exactly one job, breaking thiamine apart, which is why a fish-only diet needs a tablet to replace the loss.  The wrong choices hand the enzyme the freezer's role, the supplement's role, or symptoms the veterinarian specifically ruled out on examination.

partA.stem: Why does the memo say a fish frozen a year ago is not the same food as a fish frozen last month?
choices: Because a year-old fish looks obviously different from a fresh one on the tray.
Because freezing only slows thiaminase, so more thiamine is removed the longer the fish sits.
Because older fish spends longer being cooked before it reaches the tray.
Because an animal stores thiamine for years, and the older stores run out first.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Heat does destroy thiaminase, which is why cooking would end the problem, and nobody cooks a river otter's dinner.
A fish frozen last month is not the same food as a fish frozen a year ago, even though the two look identical on the tray.
A body cannot store very much of it, so a shortage announces itself in weeks rather than years.
The longer a fish sits frozen, the more thiamine the enzyme removes.

distractorRationale.0: The memo says the two look identical on the tray, which is precisely why the paperwork matters more than what a keeper can see.
distractorRationale.2: Heat would end the problem, but an otter's fish is never cooked at all, so cooking time cannot explain the difference.
distractorRationale.3: The memo says the opposite:  a body cannot store much thiamine, so a shortage announces itself in weeks rather than years.
