items.explain: The sentence separates instinct from choice: a heron holds still because that is what a heron has, not because she weighed her options.  The wrong choices convert the same behavior into an injury, a calculation, or sleep, each of which the surrounding lines rule out.

partA.stem: Why does the narrator keep her distance instead of helping the heron herself?
choices: Because the water was too deep and the storm made wading dangerous.
Because a wild animal on the property is not the sanctuary's animal to treat.
Because Whitlock had not yet arrived to give her permission.
Because a heron's bill is dangerous and no keeper will approach one.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Whitlock reached her by telephone at 7:22.
I found her from the boardwalk, thirty feet out in the shallow water, standing exactly where no heron in her right mind stands during a storm.
The bill goes into the towel first, which she told me afterward is the part nobody forgets, because a heron's bill is a spear and it is aimed at your face.
A wild animal that lands on our property is not our animal.

distractorRationale.0: The bird was standing in shallow water thirty feet out, so depth is not what stopped the narrator from going to her.
distractorRationale.2: Whitlock is already on the telephone with the rehabilitator;  the limit is the sanctuary's licensing, not who is standing on the boardwalk.
distractorRationale.3: The bill is genuinely dangerous, and Alva handles it anyway;  the reason the narrator waits is licensing rather than fear.

items.explain: The sanctuary cares for the residents in its files, and a wild bird belongs to a different set of rules, so the narrator's whole job is distance, sight, and a phone call.  The wrong choices substitute deep water, a missing supervisor, or fear of the bill for the rule she actually cites.

partA.stem: What do Alva's four questions on the telephone show about how she works?
choices: She is deciding whether the bird is worth the forty-minute drive.
She is checking whether the sanctuary followed its own paperwork rules.
She wants the bird's condition and how much it has already been disturbed.
She is more interested in the weather than in the bird's injuries.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: At the van she filled out a transfer slip on the hood, in the rain, with the crate already loaded, and the time she wrote on it was 8:40.
A bird that runs from you in a storm is a bird with a second injury.
That somebody is Alva Reyes, a licensed wildlife rehabilitator who lives forty minutes from here and has taken birds from us before.
How close had anybody approached it, and how long ago.

distractorRationale.0: The drive is long, but she says she is on her way immediately;  the questions come before that answer, not instead of it.
distractorRationale.1: The paperwork comes later, at the van;  her questions on the telephone are entirely about the bird and the people near it.
distractorRationale.3: The storm matters to her only through the bird:  a frightened bird moving in weather like that collects a second injury.

items.explain: Whether the bird is standing, whether it is in water, and how recently anybody came near it are all questions about condition and stress, which is what she can act on from forty minutes away.  The wrong choices read her as weighing the trip, auditing paperwork, or watching the weather instead.

partA.stem: According to Ferris, why do keepers not name a wild bird passing through?
choices: Because a name would have to be added to the sanctuary's inventory.
Because naming her starts a story that fills in what nobody actually knows.
Because the rehabilitator will give the bird a name of her own.
Because names are reserved for animals that have been at the sanctuary four years.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: Juniper's name sits at the top of a page holding four years of her weights, her burrow map, and the note that told a panicking new keeper where to look.
Alva is not required to tell us, and we are not entitled to ask her.
The moment you name a wild animal, you begin telling a story about her, and the story quietly manufactures the parts you do not actually know.
A wild bird passing through gets a date, a species, and a set of initials.

distractorRationale.0: A passing bird does get an entry, just a factual one;  the objection is to the story a name starts, not to the filing.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says the sanctuary will not learn what happens next at all, so nobody here knows what the rehabilitator calls the bird.
distractorRationale.3: Juniper's four years illustrate what a name anchors;  the rule is about residents rather than about a minimum length of stay.

items.explain: Ferris argues that a name invites invention, brave, heading home, back in the spring, and invention is what a record cannot afford.  The wrong choices turn his reasoning into a filing rule, a handoff to the rehabilitator, or a four-year waiting period the passage never sets.

partA.stem: What does the narrator mean by calling the refusal to name the heron the hardest kind of respect?
choices: Respect means keeping a wild bird's record shorter than a resident's.
Restraint looks like indifference from outside, even when it is the opposite.
She respects the rehabilitator more than she respects the bird.
Naming an animal is disrespectful in every situation.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: There is one line about her in the daily log, and there is a carbon copy of a slip that somebody else signed, and that is the whole of it.
Every animal in our files has a name, and the names are not decoration.
Alva is not required to tell us, and we are not entitled to ask her.
It is the hardest kind, because from the outside it looks exactly like not caring.

distractorRationale.0: The short record follows from the rule, but the closing line is about how the restraint looks to other people, not about length.
distractorRationale.2: Not being entitled to ask is part of the same restraint;  the sentence is about the bird, not about ranking people.
distractorRationale.3: Residents are named on purpose, and the passage calls those names load-bearing rather than disrespectful.

items.explain: The narrator names the cost of the discipline: it produces no visible sign of caring, which is why she calls it the hardest kind of respect.  The wrong choices flatten it into physical distance, into a comparison between people, or into a rule against naming any animal at all.

items.stem: Choose the three things the narrator actually did on the night she found the heron.
choices: She kept her distance and kept the bird in sight.
She wrote down the rehabilitator's instruction word for word.
She carried the carbon copy of the transfer slip back to the binder.
She threw a towel over the bird to keep it calm until help arrived.
She carried the bird up to the maintenance gate to wait for the van.

distractorRationale.3: She lists throwing a towel over the bird as one of the things she specifically did not do;  Alva uses the towel later.
distractorRationale.4: She never attempted to carry the bird anywhere at all, and Alva collects it from the water herself.

items.explain: Her whole role that night was distance, sight, a written-down instruction, and the paperwork afterward, which is what the sanctuary is actually permitted to do.  The two wrong choices are drawn from the list of actions she names and rejects in the same paragraph.

items.stem: Select the three statements that describe how this passage is written.
choices: It compares the wind to shoves rather than to gusts.
It describes human things without naming them, because the bird has no words for them.
It compares the sound of wind in the reeds to breathing.
It quotes the keeper who finds the bird at the end.
It explains the bird's injury using the words a veterinarian would use.

distractorRationale.3: A voice travels out into the darkness at the end, but the passage never gives its words;  the bird hears steadiness rather than sentences.
distractorRationale.4: The injury is described only as a wing that will not fold in and will not lift, which is what the bird can feel rather than a diagnosis.

items.explain: The passage stays inside what a heron can perceive, so wind becomes shoves, reeds become breathing, and a sanctuary becomes lights strung in a row.  The two wrong choices import a quoted human voice and medical vocabulary, both of which this point of view deliberately withholds.

items.stem: Tap the three phrases that describe air or wind as though it were solid or alive.  The other two are plain description.
spans: the air had been a road underneath her
in shoves rather than in gusts
a sound like the entire marsh breathing at once
black and wrinkling
low and yellow
items.explain: Air becomes a road she travels on, wind arrives in shoves the way a body pushes, and the reeds turn the storm into something breathing.  The last two phrases describe how water and a lamp actually look, without turning either one into something else.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state her stillness is instinct rather than something she chose.
spans: Standing still is not a decision for her;  standing still is what she is.
A heron out in the open holds still until stillness stops working.
She stood in eight inches of cold water with the rain arriving sideways and did not move for a long time.
The light stayed where it was, at a distance.
She could feel her wing as a heaviness that would not fold in and would not lift.
items.explain: One sentence denies that stillness is a decision at all, and the next explains it as what a heron in the open simply does.  The other spans show her standing in the water, the keeper keeping back, and the wing she can feel, which are the scene rather than the claim about instinct.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the rule limiting what the sanctuary is allowed to do for this bird.
spans: A wild animal that lands on our property is not our animal.
We are not licensed to treat wild birds.
Whitlock reached her by telephone at 7:22.
Her van pulled up to the maintenance gate a little after eight, in rain that was coming down flat.
It took her under a minute.
items.explain: The rule has two halves, one about ownership and one about licensing, and together they explain why a keeper who could physically reach the bird does not.  The other three spans are events that follow from the rule: the call, the van, and how quickly the rehabilitator worked once she arrived.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that give the two separate reasons a wild bird gets no name.
spans: The moment you name a wild animal, you begin telling a story about her, and the story quietly manufactures the parts you do not actually know.
A record that says Willow means whatever the reader would like it to mean.
Every animal in our files has a name, and the names are not decoration.
I do not know how she is.
The heron never got a name.
items.explain: Ferris supplies the first reason, that a name starts a story which invents what nobody knows, and Whitlock supplies the second, that outside readers cannot use a nickname.  The other spans explain why residents ARE named, admit what the narrator does not know, and simply state the fact the passage sets out to explain.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  Because the passage stays inside what the heron can sense, the sanctuary reaches her as {{0}}, and her injury reaches her as {{1}}.

choices: a place she has visited in other seasons
a line of small cold lights strung in a row
a marsh she recognises from the air
a wing that will not fold in and will not lift
a strain the rehabilitator will later diagnose
a broken bone she can feel grinding

items.explain: A heron has no word for a wildlife sanctuary, so the place arrives as lights strung in a row like something a person decided on, and the reader supplies the meaning she cannot.  The injury arrives the same way, as weight and refusal rather than as a diagnosis: a wing that will not fold in and will not lift.  She does not recognise this ground at all, and no name for the damage exists anywhere inside her point of view.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The keeper stays back because {{0}}, and the night ends for the sanctuary with {{1}}.

choices: the water is too deep to wade out safely
a wild bird that lands here is not the sanctuary's animal to treat
she is afraid of the bird's bill
a promise that the rehabilitator will telephone with news
the heron moved into an empty enclosure until morning
a signed transfer slip and a carbon copy for the binder

items.explain: The sanctuary cares for the residents in its files and is not licensed to treat wild birds, so the keeper's whole job is distance, sight, and a telephone call to somebody whose license covers this.  The file closes with the signed slip and its carbon copy, which is the last thing the sanctuary will ever record about the bird.  The water was shallow, the bill is a hazard the rehabilitator handles anyway, and nobody is owed a call about how the heron does next.

items.stem: What has the heron used to hold her line down the valley before tonight?
choices: The river for direction, the trees for edges, and the light for timing
A memory of the count of days between journeys
The lights of the places people have built
The wind, which usually pushes her the right way

distractorRationale.1: The passage says counting is not a thing she does, which is the opening line's point.
distractorRationale.2: Those lights are unfamiliar when they appear, one of the shapes she remembers nothing about.
distractorRationale.3: The wind is what takes the route away from her;  before tonight the air is described as a road, not a push.

items.explain: Her navigation is landscape and light: a river to follow, cottonwoods to edge it, and the changing light to say when to travel.  The wrong answers give her a calendar, human landmarks she does not recognise, and a wind that is the night's antagonist.

items.stem: Why does the passage say water is the one thing she can always read?
choices: She can see fish in it even from a height
It is the only thing below her she still recognises once the valley is gone
It is the safest surface for a heron to land on
It reflects the lights and shows her where people are

distractorRationale.0: No hunting appears in this passage at all;  she is trying to get down, not to feed.
distractorRationale.2: Her landing is broken by reeds and described as too fast and crooked, so safety is not what the line promises.
distractorRationale.3: The water lies beyond the lights and is described separately, black and wrinkling rather than reflective.

items.explain: Everything else below her has become shapes she has no memory of, so water is the last piece of legible landscape she has.  The wrong answers offer hunting, safety, and reflection, none of which the passage claims in a paragraph about being lost.

items.stem: Why does Alva tell the keeper not to chase the bird?
choices: A chased bird will leave the property before she arrives
Chasing would count as treating the bird without a license
A frightened bird moving in a storm collects a second injury
The bird would be too tired to travel by the time she came

distractorRationale.0: The reason she gives is about harm to the bird, not about losing track of it.
distractorRationale.1: The licensing rule is Whitlock's, and it is about care;  Alva's instruction is practical advice about injury.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing about the journey ahead is mentioned;  the concern is a fresh injury on top of the existing one.

items.explain: She states the reason in one line: a bird that runs from you in a storm is a bird with a second injury.  The wrong answers substitute a practical worry about escape, a licensing question, or a concern about travel, none of which she raises.

items.stem: What does the narrator notice about how Alva handles the heron?
choices: She works fast and loudly to startle the bird into the crate
She waits for the bird to walk into the crate on its own
She asks the keeper to hold the towel while she lifts
She approaches from the side, talking low, and secures the bill first

distractorRationale.0: She works quietly and moves in a way that makes her look slower than she is;  startling is the opposite of the method described.
distractorRationale.1: The whole handling takes under a minute and is something she does, not something she waits for.
distractorRationale.2: The keeper is not involved in the handling at all, which is the point of the licensing rule.

items.explain: The method is deliberate: side rather than front, a low voice that has nothing to do with words, the bill into the towel first because it is a spear aimed at the face.  Each wrong answer substitutes noise, passivity, or a second pair of hands the passage rules out.

items.stem: Calling a name an anchor for a record suggests what about the names in the files?
choices: They hold a history together so it can be found and added to
They keep an animal from being moved to another sanctuary
They weigh a file down with detail nobody needs
They make an animal easier for visitors to remember

distractorRationale.1: The image is about records rather than about where an animal lives;  no transfer of a resident is discussed.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says the names are not decoration, treating them as load-bearing rather than as clutter.
distractorRationale.3: Visitors never enter the reasoning;  the readers named are rehabilitators, inspectors, and whoever asks for a summary.

items.explain: Juniper's name sits at the top of four years of weights, a burrow map, and the note that saved a panicking keeper, which is exactly what an anchor does: it gives accumulated history one place to hang.  The wrong answers read the image as being about ownership, clutter, or public appeal.

items.stem: How does the narrator handle the fact that she will never learn how the heron does?
choices: She decides the bird recovered and returned to the river
She states it plainly and admits she still looks for the bird each night
She arranges for the rehabilitator to send word
She concludes that not knowing proves the rule is wrong

distractorRationale.0: That is precisely the invented ending Ferris warns against, and she names her own pull toward it as something to resist.
distractorRationale.2: She says Alva is not required to tell them, and treats the news as not theirs to ask for.
distractorRationale.3: She calls the restraint a kind of respect, and the hardest kind, rather than evidence against it.

items.explain: The entry holds two things at once: the discipline is right, and it costs something she keeps paying on every round.  The wrong answers resolve that tension by inventing an ending, arranging news nobody owes her, or abandoning the rule.

items.stem: Put the events of the heron's night in the order the journal records them.
tiles: A transfer slip is filled out on the hood of the van
A light finds a heron standing thirty feet out in the shallows
The rehabilitator asks four questions by telephone
A towel goes over the bill in under a minute
items.explain: The night runs from discovery to telephone call to handling to paperwork, and each step waits on the one before it.  Putting the slip or the handling earlier would skip the licensing rule that makes the phone call, rather than the keeper, the next move after finding the bird.

items.stem: Put the stages of the heron's flight in the order the passage moves through them.
tiles: The ground below turns into shapes she has no memory of
The air holds steady enough to travel on all afternoon
Reeds break a landing that comes in too fast and crooked
Wind arrives from the wrong side of the sky in shoves
items.explain: The passage is built as a loss in four stages: a reliable afternoon, a wind that takes it away, unfamiliar ground once the valley is gone, and finally the landing.  Reordering it would break the cause and effect, because each stage is what makes the next one possible.

partA.stem: Two sources disagree about when the van left with the heron.  Which one settles it, and why?
choices: Tanaka's account, because he was on the property and saw the van himself.
Neither, because a disagreement between two sources cannot be resolved.
The transfer slip, because it carries a time and two signatures and his memory carries neither.
Tanaka's account, because the wind readings show the wind rose after he says the van left.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Nine o'clock reads 44 miles an hour, and the margin records the night's peak gust, 52 miles an hour at 9:20 p.m.
The slip carries a time and two signatures, while his memory carries neither, and he is the first person to say so.
The recollection belongs to Wes Tanaka, who was on the property until nine and wrote nothing down.
Build one page that puts every record of the night of the twenty-sixth of May in order, and mark every place where they disagree.

distractorRationale.0: Being present is not the same as recording anything;  the page notes he wrote nothing down that night.
distractorRationale.1: Marking a disagreement is the first step, not the last;  the page then weighs the two sources against each other.
distractorRationale.3: The wind grid records what the wind did, which cannot confirm a departure time nobody wrote down at the moment it happened.

items.explain: A signed slip fixes a time at the moment of the event, while a recollection fixes it days later, and Tanaka is the first to admit the difference.  The wrong choices treat presence as documentation, treat any disagreement as unresolvable, or ask the wind grid to answer a question about people.

partA.stem: What does the blank eight o'clock line on the pin sheet establish?
choices: That the required second check of every service gate pin was never initialed.
That the gates were never pinned at any point that evening.
That somebody removed the pin from the north service gate before eight.
That the sheet beside the keeper room door was never printed for that night.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: The gate log shows the last visitor vehicle out at 7:40 p.m., and the pedestrian gate pinned and initialed at 7:44 p.m.
The sheet for the twenty-sixth of May has a printed line for eight o'clock and nothing written on it.
Bulletin 14 requires a second check of every service gate pin at 8 p.m., initialed on the sheet beside the keeper room door.
At 10:05 p.m. Ferris reported the north service gate standing open, with its latch pin lying in the mud below the hinge, bent.

distractorRationale.1: The gate log records the pedestrian gate pinned and initialed at 7:44, so the first round of pinning did happen and was signed for.
distractorRationale.2: The pin turns up in the mud two hours later, and the page says explicitly that no record can say how it came out.
distractorRationale.3: The sheet exists and carries a printed line for eight o'clock;  what is missing is the initials, not the form.

items.explain: An empty line on a sheet that has a printed row for that hour is evidence of an omission, which is a narrower claim than knowing what happened at the gate.  The wrong choices stretch the blank into unpinned gates, into a person removing a pin, or into a missing form.

partA.stem: What does the narrator say the timeline cannot settle, and why not?
choices: When the fence gap was found, because only one keeper was present.
How the pin came out of the gate, because nobody wrote it down or saw it.
Whether the heron left with a licensed rehabilitator, because memories conflict.
What the wind was doing at nine o'clock, because the grid was filled in later.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: It can settle that the heron left with a licensed rehabilitator at 8:40 p.m., because a signed slip outweighs a memory.
It cannot say how the pin came out of that gate, because no record was written while it was happening and nobody saw it.
Nine o'clock reads 44 miles an hour, and the margin records the night's peak gust, 52 miles an hour at 9:20 p.m.
It can settle when the gap was found and who found it, because two separate records agree.

distractorRationale.0: The gap is one of the things the page can settle, precisely because two separate records agree about it.
distractorRationale.2: The transfer slip settles that question;  the conflicting memory is exactly what the signed record outweighs.
distractorRationale.3: The grid carries an hourly reading for nine o'clock and a peak gust in the margin, so the wind is among the settled facts.

items.explain: The page draws its own boundary: it can order events that were recorded and cannot explain an event nobody recorded or witnessed.  Each wrong choice picks a question the records do answer and treats it as open, which is the mistake the closing lines are written to prevent.

partA.stem: Why can the page settle when the gap in Fence Nine was found?
choices: Because the newspaper published the time two days afterward.
Because the keeper who found it remembers the moment clearly.
Because the work order and the radio log were written by the same person.
Because two separate records agree about the time and the finder.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: Build one page that puts every record of the night of the twenty-sixth of May in order, and mark every place where they disagree.
It can settle when the gap was found and who found it, because two separate records agree.
At 9:52 p.m. I reported the gap in Fence Nine at post fourteen.
Work order 318 opens at 10:30 p.m. and closes the fence with a temporary panel.

distractorRationale.0: The page is built from the sanctuary's own records;  the newspaper is not among the five sources it lists.
distractorRationale.1: The radio log entry is what fixes the time;  a clear memory of the same moment is not what the page relies on.
distractorRationale.2: The two records are separate documents opened at different times, and it is that documentary corroboration the page leans on rather than a shared author.

items.explain: Agreement between two independently written records is what raises a claim from an assertion to a settled fact on this page.  The wrong choices lean on the newspaper, on a keeper's memory of her own report, or on a shared author that would actually weaken the agreement.

partA.stem: What is the second step of the morning report's argument, and what supports it?
choices: That the open gate was a procedure failure, supported by the blank eight o'clock line.
That the open gate was an equipment failure, supported by the bent latch pin.
That the fence failure was not a failure of upkeep, supported by the inspection line.
That nothing went wrong that night, supported by the animal count closing before eleven.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The sanctuary's defense is not that nothing went wrong, because something plainly did.
The second step is that the open gate was a failure of procedure, whatever the equipment did.
The report supports that step with the blank eight o'clock line rather than with anybody's opinion.
The first step is that the fence failure was not a failure of upkeep.

distractorRationale.1: The report names procedure rather than equipment, and it refuses to say anything at all about how the pin came out.
distractorRationale.2: That is the report's first step;  the question asks for the second, which concerns the gate rather than the fence.
distractorRationale.3: The report says the opposite in its third step:  something plainly did go wrong, and the defense rests on it being written down.

items.explain: The report separates its claim from its support at every step, and the second step rests on an absence, the uninitialed eight o'clock line, rather than on anybody's opinion.  The wrong choices swap in the first step, an equipment theory the report refuses, or a denial it explicitly rejects.

partA.stem: What is the central claim the morning report finally makes?
choices: That the sanctuary handled the storm without anything going wrong.
That the newspaper is responsible for the damage to the sanctuary's reputation.
That everything which went wrong was written down by the people it went wrong for.
That a record protects the keeper who wrote it from being blamed later.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage is the best evidence for that answer?
choices: It does not argue about the headline, and it never complains about the unnamed neighbor.
The defense is that everything which went wrong was written down by the people it went wrong for.
A record is not a defense of the person who wrote it.
The sanctuary's defense is not that nothing went wrong, because something plainly did.

distractorRationale.0: The report concedes immediately that something went wrong;  denying it is the position the third step is written against.
distractorRationale.1: The attached letter asks only for a correction of two claims and deliberately avoids arguing about the headline or the neighbor.
distractorRationale.3: The closing lines say a record is not a defense of its writer at all;  it is a promise to whoever reads it next.

items.explain: The report trades the claim of a perfect night for a stronger one: the failures are visible in the sanctuary's own paper, written by the people they happened to.  The wrong choices claim perfection, blame the newspaper, or turn the record into personal protection the last lines reject.

partA.stem: How does the attached letter to the newspaper make its case?
choices: It disputes the headline and the use of an unnamed neighbor as a source.
It demands that the newspaper print the sanctuary's morning report in full.
It names two claims and cites the record that contradicts each one.
It argues that a newspaper should not report on the sanctuary without permission.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage most directly backs up your answer?
choices: It names two claims, along with the record that contradicts each one.
It does not argue about the headline, and it never complains about the unnamed neighbor.
The letter asks for nothing else.
The last section is a letter, and Whitlock attached a copy of it.

distractorRationale.0: The letter deliberately leaves both alone, which is what keeps it to the two claims a record can actually settle.
distractorRationale.1: The letter asks for a correction and nothing else at all, so it makes no demand about printing the report.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the letter challenges the newspaper's right to report;  it challenges two specific sentences with two specific records.

items.explain: The letter answers a claim with a document each time, the twelfth of May inspection line and Bulletin 14, and asks for nothing beyond the correction.  The wrong choices widen it into a fight about the headline, the newspaper's sources, or its right to report at all.

partA.stem: Bulletin 14 asked several things of the evening shift.  Which one do the night's records show was never written down?
choices: Reading the wind station and logging what it showed.
The second check of every service gate pin at eight o'clock.
Sending keepers out in pairs for the rest of the evening.
Pinning the pedestrian gate once the last visitor had gone.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage would you cite to defend that answer?
choices: No initials appear anywhere in that row.
The gate log shows the last visitor vehicle out at 7:40 p.m., and the pedestrian gate pinned and initialed at 7:44 p.m.
The radio log also records Ferris sending every keeper out in pairs at 8:05 p.m., exactly as the bulletin asked.
The wind station grid runs alongside all of this.

distractorRationale.0: The grid runs right through the evening and carries the night's peak gust, so those readings were taken and written down.
distractorRationale.2: The radio log records Ferris sending every keeper out in pairs at 8:05, so that instruction was carried out and written down.
distractorRationale.3: The gate log shows that gate pinned and initialed at 7:44, which is the same two-part record the eight o'clock line is missing.

items.explain: The page shows three of the bulletin's tasks carried out and written down, and one row on the pin sheet with no initials in it anywhere.  Each wrong choice names a task some record in the timeline positively confirms, which is the difference between a task nobody did and a task nobody logged.

items.stem: Choose the three sources that belong to the five records covering the night of the storm.
choices: The gate log.
Work order 318.
The signed transfer slip for the heron.
Wes Tanaka's recollection of the van leaving.
The Valley Register article about the fence.

distractorRationale.3: Tanaka's recollection is the one account on the page that is not a record;  he was present until nine and wrote nothing down.
distractorRationale.4: The newspaper article is an outside source published two days later and is not among the five records the page assembles.

items.explain: The five records are the gate log, the radio log, the wind station grid, work order 318, and the signed transfer slip, all written during the night itself.  The two wrong choices are the memory the page weighs against those records and an outside article written afterward.

items.stem: Select the three changes the morning report puts in place.
choices: The pin check gains a second initial column.
The wind station grid is filled in by whoever walks rounds.
The volunteer log gains a line asking what you heard and when you wrote it down.
Night rounds move an hour earlier during storm season.
The maintenance binder is closed to anyone outside the sanctuary.

distractorRationale.3: No change to the timing of rounds appears anywhere;  the three changes all concern who writes a record and when.
distractorRationale.4: The report moves in the opposite direction, using its own records openly, including in a correction letter sent to a newspaper.

items.explain: Each change repairs the exact record that failed: a second initial for the pin check, a named writer for the wind grid, and a timing line for the volunteer log.  The two wrong choices reschedule rounds and hide the binder, neither of which follows from the report's findings.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that state something this page CAN settle.
spans: It can settle when the gap was found and who found it, because two separate records agree.
It can settle that the heron left with a licensed rehabilitator at 8:40 p.m., because a signed slip outweighs a memory.
It can settle that the eight o'clock pin check was never initialed, because the line for it is empty.
It cannot say how the pin came out of that gate, because no record was written while it was happening and nobody saw it.
A timeline is not a witness.
items.explain: Three sentences name settled questions and give the reason each is settled: two records agreeing, a signed slip outweighing a memory, and an empty line where initials belong.  The last two mark the boundary instead, naming the question no record can answer and why a timeline cannot testify.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that draw the line between a record and a recollection.
spans: Five records cover that night, and one recollection does not.
The slip carries a time and two signatures, while his memory carries neither, and he is the first person to say so.
Tanaka remembers that van differently.
The wind station grid runs alongside all of this.
At 10:05 p.m. Ferris reported the north service gate standing open, with its latch pin lying in the mud below the hinge, bent.
items.explain: The first sentence sorts the night's sources into records and one recollection, and the second explains what actually separates them: a time and two signatures against neither.  The others report that the memory differs, and give two entries from the timeline itself.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the first two steps of the report's argument.
spans: The first step is that the fence failure was not a failure of upkeep.
The second step is that the open gate was a failure of procedure, whatever the equipment did.
The third step ties the whole stack of paper together.
The report says nothing whatsoever about how the pin came out, which is the sentence I would have been most tempted to write.
This one ran to two full pages.
items.explain: The report numbers its own argument, and the first two steps make claims about the fence and about the gate.  The third span announces a step without stating it, the fourth describes a deliberate silence, and the fifth is the length of the document.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that name a change the report actually puts in place.
spans: The pin check gains a second initial column, exactly like the supplement column on a diet card.
The wind station grid gets filled in by whoever is walking rounds, rather than by whoever remembers at the end of the night.
The volunteer log gains a new line at the top of every entry, asking what you heard and when you wrote it down.
The letter asks for nothing else.
A record is not a defense of the person who wrote it.
items.explain: Each change repairs the record that failed that night: a second initial for the pin check, a named writer for the wind grid, and a timing line for the volunteer log.  The other two spans describe the correction letter's restraint and the closing idea about what a record is for.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The timeline settles {{0}}, and it leaves open {{1}}.

choices: why the storm brought the willow limb down
which keeper found the fence gap, and at what time
whether the newspaper will print a correction
how the latch pin came out of the north service gate
what time the heron left with the rehabilitator
whether the eight o'clock pin check was initialed

items.explain: Two separate records agree about the gap, so its time and its finder are settled;  a signed slip settles the heron's departure at 8:40, and an empty printed line settles that the eight o'clock check went uninitialed.  What no record covers is how the pin came out, because nobody wrote anything while it was happening and nobody saw it.  The storm damage and the newspaper's response are simply not questions this page was built to answer.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The report argues the open gate was {{0}}, and its defence of the sanctuary is that {{1}}.

choices: a step somebody skipped rather than a part that broke
the result of a bent pin that should have been replaced
nobody's fault, given the strength of the wind
the storm was severe enough to excuse the damage
nothing actually went wrong that night
everything that went wrong was written down by the people it happened to

items.explain: The second step of the argument rests on the blank eight o'clock line rather than on anybody's opinion, which makes the open gate a procedure failure;  the report deliberately says nothing about how the pin came out.  Its third step then trades the claim of a perfect night for a stronger one, that every failure is visible in the sanctuary's own paper.  Blaming the equipment, excusing the wind, or denying that anything went wrong are all positions the report explicitly declines to take.

items.stem: What is the assignment behind this page?
choices: Decide who was responsible for the open gate
Summarise the night for the newspaper's correction
Put every record of the night in order and mark where they disagree
Establish which witness account was the most accurate

distractorRationale.0: The page names an uninitialed check and stops;  it refuses to say how the pin came out, let alone who is at fault.
distractorRationale.1: The correction letter is attached to the morning report, and it cites two records rather than this timeline.
distractorRationale.3: Only one recollection is involved here, and it is weighed against a signed slip rather than against other witnesses.

items.explain: Whitlock's instruction is a single sentence, and it asks for two things: order, and the places where sources conflict.  Everything the page can and cannot settle follows from taking that assignment literally rather than reaching for a culprit or an audience.

items.stem: What is the first radio log entry that matters to this timeline?
choices: The last visitor vehicle leaving the property
The gap in Fence Nine at post fourteen
Bulletin 14 going up on the keeper room door
A heron reported down in the marsh with one wing carried wrong

distractorRationale.0: That is the gate log rather than the radio log, and it comes later, at 7:40.
distractorRationale.1: That entry comes at 9:52, more than two hours into the evening the page reconstructs.
distractorRationale.2: The bulletin is posted at four o'clock and is not a radio entry at all.

items.explain: The evening begins on paper with the bulletin, but the radio log's first meaningful entry is the heron at 7:15, which is what makes the transfer slip part of this night's record.  The wrong answers pick real events from the timeline that belong to other records or later hours.

items.stem: Why does the page include a recollection at all, when it has five records?
choices: It is one of the places the sources disagree, which the assignment asks for
It fills a gap none of the five records covers
It is the only account from somebody who was present
It corrects a time the slip records incorrectly

distractorRationale.1: The transfer slip covers the same moment with a time and two signatures, so the memory adds no new ground.
distractorRationale.2: The keepers who wrote the radio log and the gate log were present too, and they wrote at the time.
distractorRationale.3: The comparison runs the other way:  the slip carries a time and signatures, the memory carries neither, and Tanaka says so himself.

items.explain: The assignment asks for every place the sources disagree, so a recollection that conflicts with a signed slip belongs on the page precisely because it loses.  Recording the conflict is what lets a later reader see that the question was asked and settled.

items.stem: The narrator says the report leaves out the sentence she would most have wanted to write.  What is it?
choices: A defence of the keeper who missed the eight o'clock check
An explanation of how the latch pin came out of the gate
An accusation aimed at the newspaper
A claim that the storm was worse than the advisory predicted

distractorRationale.0: The report does not defend anybody;  it records the blank line and builds a change from it.
distractorRationale.2: The attached letter is deliberately narrow, asking for a correction on two claims and nothing more.
distractorRationale.3: The wind readings are simply logged, and the report never argues about severity.

items.explain: The tempting sentence is the causal one, because a cause makes a report feel finished, and the report refuses it because no record supports it.  Each wrong answer names something the report also does not do, but none is the sentence the narrator admits she wanted.

items.stem: Why does the pin check get a second initial column, of all the possible fixes?
choices: Two keepers should be present whenever a gate is pinned
The old sheet had no line for eight o'clock at all
One signature was covering two separate jobs, exactly as on a diet card
Initials are easier to check than a written time

distractorRationale.0: The change is about two tasks rather than two people, which is the same design the diet card uses for fish and tablet.
distractorRationale.1: The line was printed and simply left blank, which is what made the omission visible.
distractorRationale.3: The report never compares formats;  it identifies which record failed and repairs that record.

items.explain: The fix is borrowed from a case two levels earlier: when one initial can cover two jobs, the job people forget is the one that goes unrecorded.  Splitting the column makes the omission visible the same night rather than in a report afterward.

items.stem: What does the report's last line say a record is for?
choices: Protecting the keeper who filled it in from later blame
Satisfying an inspector who may ask for it
Proving that the sanctuary followed every procedure
The person who reads it next, rather than the person who wrote it

distractorRationale.0: The line says explicitly that a record is not a defence of the person who wrote it.
distractorRationale.1: Inspectors are named elsewhere as readers, but the closing line is broader than any one audience.
distractorRationale.2: The report has just conceded a procedure that was missed, so proving compliance cannot be the claim.

items.explain: The closing line turns a record from a shield into an obligation owed forward, which is the same idea the very first level states as a rule about honesty at the moment of writing.  The wrong answers each make the record serve its author or an audit rather than the next reader.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, what is the one thing this timeline cannot settle?
accept: how the latch pin came out
how the latch pin got out
how the pin came out of the gate
how the pin got out of the gate
how the pin came out of that gate
how the gate pin came out
